summaries.summary: Twitter faces widespread online harassment, especially toward women, motivating automated sexual harassment content detection to reduce human effort and flag or remove hate speech.
Previous studies addressed sexism and racism broadly or used benevolent and hostile sexism, with little focus on different online harassment types using natural language processing.

This work participates in the SociaL Media And Harassment Competition of the ECML PKDD 2019 Conference, using competition tweet data and attention-based Recurrent Neural Networks for two classification tasks.

Prior work categorized hateful tweets as sexist, racist or neither, then developed broader sexism and online harassment categories including indirect harassment, information threat, sexual harassment, physical harassment and not sexist.

Related hate speech detection approaches include SVMs, RNNs, FastText, SemEval2018 evaluations, text augmentation, convolutional and gated recurrent networks, ensemble RNN classifiers, and several attention mechanisms.
The Twitter dataset has train, validation and test sets, harassment and non-harassment categories, three harassment sub-categories, and imbalance affecting results.
Back-translation of indirect and physical harassment train tweets from english to german, french and greek and back augments data and boosts model performance.
Pre-trained word embeddings from 2B Twitter data having 27B tokens initialize the embedding layer.
A tweet pre-processor cleans and tokenizes the dataset before model training.
The attention-based approach uses RNN models with GRU cells and an LR Layer to classify tweets as harassment or non-harassment and other categories.
The paragraph defines GRU hidden state computation terms, gates, functions, matrices, biases, and the LR Layer probability estimate for harassment.
An attention mechanism similar to BIBREF9 makes the LR Layer consider the weighted sum h_sum of all hidden states instead of h_k.
The weighted sum is defined as h_sum = sum from t=1 to k of alpha_t h_t.
The attention RNN probability is defined as P_attentionRNN = sigma(W_p h_sum + b_p).
Alternatively, h_sum can pass through an MLP with k layers before the LR layer estimates the corresponding probability.
The alternative attention RNN probability is defined as P_attentionRNN = sigma(W_p h_* + b_p).
The classification-specific attention mechanism uses four attention mechanisms, one per category, assigns larger weights to harassment evidence, and adds a projection layer for word embeddings.
The architecture uses 200-dimensional pre-trained Twitter embeddings, Spatial Dropout, a 128-unit tanh MLP, a 128-size unidirectional GRU, four self-attentions, and a 128-node ReLU MLP.
This subsection gives training process details and describes the different models compared in the experiments.
Training uses batch size 32, epochs = 20, patience = 10, and average AUC as early stopping criterion because the dataset is imbalanced.
Training optimizes the loss function with the Adam optimizer and learning rate equal to 0.001.
The loss function is L = 1/2 BCE(harassment) + 1/2(1/5 BCE(sexualH) + 2/5 BCE(indirectH) + 2/5 BCE(physicalH)).
BCE is the binary cross-entropy loss function.
BCE is defined as -1/n sum from i=1 to n of [y_i log(y'_i) + (1 - y_i) log(1 - y'_i)].
The loss function weights both tasks equally and gives higher weight to harder harassment categories due to class imbalance among training, validation and test sets.
Each model produces four scores, and a threshold equal to 0.33 determines harassment labels and the harassment type with the greatest score.
Eight models compare LastStateRNN, AvgRNN, AttentionRNN and MultiAttentionRNN, with four having a Projected Layer and four not having one.
Models were evaluated using F1 Score averaged over ten runs, with multi-attention models outperforming others and the Projected Layer version achieving the highest F1 Macro.
The attention-based RNN approach detects harassment language and harassment types, with multi-attention and a projected layer achieving highest F1 Score and back-translation addressing imbalance.
Future work will apply BERT BIBREF21 to this dataset and apply the presented models to other hate speech datasets in social media.
